bull_thesis: Eiffage is a French infrastructure conglomerate that the market prices as if it were mostly a low-margin builder, when a large share of its profit is a toll-road annuity. The bull case rests on the gap between those two facts. The Concessions arm — above all the APRR/AREA motorway network, plus stakes in Getlink (the Channel Tunnel) and a growing set of newer concessions — produces dependable, inflation-linked cash: toll revenue of roughly 3 billion euros a year at a very high cash margin, running under contract to 2035-2036. On its own that annuity is worth a large multiple of the Contracting business it is bolted to. Around it sits a genuinely improving Contracting engine: a record, diversified order book near 30 billion euros (+3% in 2025) with multi-year visibility, deliberately re-weighted from a weak French housing market toward European energy and grid work — the Amprion North Sea grid interconnection (~2 billion euros retained share), offshore-wind substations via Smulders/HSM, the EPR2 nuclear programme (~5 billion euros in backlog), and Greater Paris Express metro contracts. Management is disciplined and shareholder-friendly: a formalised 45% dividend payout (2025 dividend 4.80 euros, up from 4.70), opportunistic buybacks that already parked ~5.8% of shares in treasury which management explicitly refuses to cancel or reverse (optionality for an accretive cancellation later), and net debt cut ~870 million euros in 2025 to ~8.5 billion even while absorbing 825 million of acquisitions. Free cash flow stayed high near 2.1 billion euros. Delivery has been steady — earnings per share compounded from 7.65 (2021) to 11.01 (2025) with no air-pocket, and beats in three of the last four quarters. Trading at a persistent discount to its closest peer Vinci on comparable concession-asset quality, the re-rating comes slowly through continued deleveraging, buybacks, and the market eventually crediting the toll-road cash for what it is. The conditions that must hold: traffic stays flat-to-up, French windfall taxation does not become permanently punitive, and the balance sheet keeps grinding lower.
bear_thesis: The discount to Vinci is not a free lunch — it is compensation for real, structural problems. First and largest: the APRR/AREA concession clock. The crown-jewel toll-road cash flows expire around 2035-2036, and what replaces them is genuinely undecided. Management itself will not guess before 2027-2028, and the French regulator is openly pushing for 'shorter periods, more regulation, review clauses.' Any sober valuation must fade the concession annuity for that finiteness and the live risk that renewal terms are far less generous — which caps how much the toll roads are worth today and removes the tidy 'sum-of-the-parts is worth more than the whole' story. Second, the Contracting base is thin and drifting: gross margin is explicitly contracting (12.9% and falling), net margin is only ~3.9%, and return on invested capital is a mediocre 6.3% — barely above a reasonable cost of capital, which means the giant construction revenue base creates little economic value on its own. Third, leverage: net debt of roughly 8.5-9.8 billion euros and an Altman-Z solvency score of 1.8 sit in the grey zone, leaving less cushion than the sturdy cash flow implies, and much of the headline 4x price-to-free-cash-flow 'cheapness' is inflated because a slice of that cash belongs to APRR minority partners and to servicing the debt. Fourth, France-specific tax and political risk is unresolved and one-sided — a ~200 million euro windfall surtax hit 2025, and (confirmed since, via the Finance Act 2026 adopted 2026-02-02) was extended into FY2026 for large-turnover companies at an even higher effective rate. Crucially, there is no hard, dated catalyst to force a re-rating: this is a slow grind that depends on the market changing its mind, and the one event that could actually move the concessions (post-2035 renewal terms) is years away and could just as easily impair value as unlock it. What confirms the bear: a punitive concession-renewal signal, traffic rolling over, or the windfall tax made permanent beyond FY2026.
consensus_delta: For a deep-value name the right question is whether the street is pricing terminal decline into a company with stable, growing earnings power. Here the answer is: only partly, and the mispricing is modest, not large. The market treats Eiffage as a leveraged French builder and applies a builder's discount to the whole enterprise — that is where it is wrong, because a large slice of profit is an inflation-linked toll-road annuity (APRR/AREA), rated A/A-, with 2.7 billion euros of cash, that deserves a far higher multiple than construction. Where the street is NOT wrong: it correctly discounts the toll roads for their 2035-2036 finiteness and the genuinely undecided renewal regime (management itself won't forecast before 2027-2028), and it correctly penalises the thin ~3.9% net margin, 6.3% return on invested capital, and grey-zone leverage. Net, our disagreement with the market is real but small — the toll-road cash is worth a bit more than credited — and it is NOT single-name alpha so much as a shared French-concessions sector discount that also sits on Vinci. There is no hidden growth engine the street is missing.
forcing_function: There is no hard, dated event that forces a re-rating — this is the crux and the reason for a wait rather than an aggressive entry. The value case depends on slow-burn mechanisms: continued buybacks, further deleveraging, and the market gradually crediting the toll-road annuity. The FY2025 annual results (delivered 2026-02-25) and the employee-share-plan-linked treasury cancellation (~2.0 million shares, completed 2026-05-19) have both already landed and are priced in — that cancellation was a routine anti-dilution offset tied to the employee plan, not the discretionary, accretive cancellation the bull case is really banking on, so the optionality remains live and uncashed. The next scheduled data point is the H1 2026 results on 2026-08-26. The single event that could genuinely re-rate (or impair) the concessions — the post-2035 APRR/AREA renewal terms and the new French concession model — will not clarify until 2027-2028 by management's own admission, and could cut either way. None of the near-term dates is binding or asymmetric. Against the current regime — which rewards hard-dated structural special-situations (spinoffs, forced-sellers, distressed) in thin-coverage lanes and penalises theses hinging on a rate rescue or a far-off macro resolution — Eiffage offers neither a dated forcing function nor resolution-driver independence (its key unknown, French concession regulation, is a single shared macro-political factor). That holds conviction to a middling level.
valley_of_death: The near-term risks are containable but real. First, French fiscal and political instability: the ~200 million euro windfall corporate surtax that hit 2025 was extended into FY2026 (Finance Act 2026, adopted 2026-02-02, ~30.98-36.30% effective CIT for qualifying large-turnover companies) — management has said it has 'no more visibility than you have' on whether this becomes a durable feature, and a permanently higher tax rate would directly cut group earnings and, via the 45% payout, the dividend. Second, traffic softness: APRR traffic was down ~0.9% in the first quarter of 2026, and a consumer or fuel-price shock would pressure the concession cash that carries the whole margin. Third, this is a rate-sensitive, leveraged infrastructure name into a hawkish-Fed / higher-for-longer regime — so there is no rate-rescue tailwind, and the debt is refinanced at higher cost. None of these is a cash-burn hump or a maturity wall that threatens solvency; free cash flow near 2.1 billion euros comfortably covers the dividend. The risk is to the multiple and the dividend, not to survival.
positioning_washout: There is no obvious forced or mechanical selling dynamic to exploit or fear. Eiffage is a large, liquid CAC-mid/large-cap held broadly by European value and income funds; the treasury stake is a stabiliser, not an overhang. The one scenario that could force yield-focused holders out is a dividend cut driven by a punitive French tax — but that is a tail risk, not a base case, and the 45% payout with ~2.1 billion euros of free cash flow gives ample cover. Equally, there is no washed-out, capitulated shareholder base to buy from: the stock sits 43% up its 52-week range and modestly below its 200-day average, so there is no forced-selling flush to lean into.
moderator_conclusion: Eiffage is a well-run, cash-generative French infrastructure compounder whose sum-of-the-parts — a rich, inflation-linked toll-road annuity welded to a thin-margin but improving Contracting engine — is worth modestly more than the market's builder-style discount credits, but not dramatically so. Our reconciled base-case value is about 135 euros a share against a spot near 122: roughly fair-to-modestly-cheap, with an adverse parts value near 105-115 and a favorable one near 150-165, for a broadly symmetric, mildly-positive risk/reward. The load-bearing catalyst is soft and non-binding: there is no dated, contractual event to force a re-rating, and the one thing that could truly move the concessions — the post-2035 renewal regime — is years away (2027-2028 visibility) and could impair as easily as unlock value. Applying the current market regime sharpens the call rather than softening it: the regime pays up for hard-dated structural special-situations with resolution-driver independence and explicitly deprioritises theses that lean on a rate rescue or a distant macro-political resolution — and Eiffage is exactly the latter, a leveraged infrastructure name whose central unknown is a single shared French-regulatory factor, into a hawkish-Fed backdrop with no rate tailwind. It is also not idiosyncratic alpha: much of the Vinci discount is a sector-wide French-concessions repricing that both names carry. The verdict is to wait for the wash-out — specifically, wait for a cleaner entry on a French-fiscal or traffic-driven flush, or for genuine clarity/optionality from a discretionary treasury-share cancellation or a constructive concession-renewal signal — rather than pay up now for a fairly-priced grind. Conviction is a middling hold. The value case, judged purely on valuation versus intrinsic worth and the quality of the forensic record and ignoring any catalyst, is the same middling level: the discount is real but shallow and partly structural, the balance sheet is leveraged, and the concessions are a narrow, finite moat — a solid but unexciting three, neither a trap nor a bargain.
sop_breakdown: Base-case ~135 euros/share, essentially in line with market price. Concessions ~90/share (APRR/AREA toll annuity valued for a shortened, uncertain remaining life to ~2035-2036 rather than perpetuity, plus Getlink and newer concessions, net of allocated parent debt) — this is the durable value core. Contracting ~50/share (~21 billion euros revenue at ~3.5% net margin, ~8x, credit for the ~30 billion euro backlog and European energy/grid re-weighting). Treasury-stock optionality and the 45% payout add a few euros of latent value. Less residual parent leverage. The parts sum to roughly the traded price — this is a fairly-priced quality compounder, not a deep discount.
risk_reward: Roughly symmetric, mildly favorable, and a touch wider now that the quote has drifted down to 121.85 from the ~130 reference at the original full debate (122.30 at the last pass). Downside-to-break ~105-115 (the adverse parts value, now ~6-14% below the 121.85 spot); upside-to-fair ~135 base (~11% above spot); upside-to-favorable ~150-165 (~23-35% above spot). At today's slightly lower quote the risk/reward skews marginally better than 1:1 (about 1.1:1) — still a hold-and-collect-the-dividend profile, not an asymmetric special-situation.
catalyst_status_plain: a soft catalyst, no fixed date
peer_comps_note: Peers: Vinci (VIE.PA, the closest true comp — same construction-plus-concessions hybrid), Bouygues (BOUY.PA), ACS/Ferrovial (FER.MC/ACS.MC), Saint-Gobain (SGO.PA). The screener flags Eiffage as cheap-versus-peers, trading at a persistent discount to Vinci on comparable concession-asset quality that looks partly structural (bigger low-margin construction mix, more leverage, the unresolved concession-renewal question) and only partly mispricing. Important discipline: the discount to Vinci is a SHARED-FACTOR French-concessions discount — both names carry the same unresolved driver (French toll-road regulation, windfall taxation, the post-2035 renewal regime), so a large part of the gap is sector beta on that one regulatory factor, NOT idiosyncratic single-name alpha. Do not credit the full Vinci discount as Eiffage-specific edge. The genuinely name-specific edge is thinner: Eiffage's heavier buyback/treasury optionality and faster deleveraging.

bull_thesis:
The bull case is that the market is applying a French-motorway discount to a company that is only half a French motorway, and pricing the rest for nothing. At 109.20 euros Eiffage is worth 10.7 billion euros. Inside that sit three things a buyer would want. First, the APRR and AREA motorway concessions, a legal monopoly generating roughly 2.3 billion euros a year of earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation at margins above 70%, inflation-linked through the tariff formula, with about nine years left to run. Second, a contracting business (construction, infrastructure and energy systems) turning over about 21.7 billion euros a year at a 4.3% operating margin, whose order book has grown every single reporting period since 2023 across every business line, and which is winning exactly the work the next decade is going to pay for: roughly 5 billion euros of new-nuclear EPR2 work in the book, a twelve-year Arabelle Solutions partnership manufacturing nuclear heat-exchanger components, a 2 billion euro grid contract for Amprion in Germany, a 25-year Greater Paris district-heating concession signed in the first half of 2026, and a 120 million euro electrical substation for an artificial-intelligence data-centre campus at Fouju. Third, a stake of roughly 20% in Getlink, the Channel Tunnel operator, worth about 2.05 billion euros at Getlink's 18.89 euro share price today, or a fifth of Eiffage's entire market value, carried in the accounts far below that and marked at a price near Getlink's own 52-week high.

The operating evidence supports it. Europe outside France still grew more than 8% in the first half of 2026 (4.7% organically) while France stalled, which is the German, Dutch, Spanish, Belgian and Polish build-out of 2024 and 2025 doing precisely what it was bought to do. Operating margins improved to 8.2% from 8.0% even as revenue growth fell to 1.0%, so the slowdown is a volume story, not a pricing or execution story. Management has delivered three consecutive guidance commitments, has flagged every disappointment in the call it occurred rather than after, and has been actively deflating its own hottest narrative: asked about a 30 billion euro European data-centre opportunity, the chief executive spent several minutes arguing it down, noting he has two teams in France capable of a hyperscale project and that European permitting is slower than anyone expects. That is unusual and creditable behaviour in a market where Hochtief trades at 36 times earnings substantially on data-centre enthusiasm.

The valuation lever is straightforward. Corrected for the data error, Eiffage trades at 9.8 times trailing earnings and about 5.1 times enterprise value to EBITDA, against Vinci at 12.5 times earnings and 6.5 times, and Bouygues at 13.5 times. Eiffage yields 4.40% against Vinci's 4.38%, so an investor is paid the same to wait while owning the cheaper asset. Closing even part of that gap, on unchanged earnings, is worth 20% or more. The conditions that must hold are specific: oil has to come off its current 91 dollars so light-vehicle motorway traffic recovers; the French state has to refrain from a further permanent levy on infrastructure beyond the existing long-distance transport tax and the temporary corporate surtax; and the contracting order book has to convert at the 4-5% operating margin management insists is unchanged. If all three hold, the parts are worth around 175 euros.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is that Eiffage is cheap for four reasons that are all real, and that the cheapness is smaller than it looks.

Start with the arithmetic, because it is where most bulls go wrong. The headline 3.6 times free cash flow that makes this stock screen as extraordinary is an artefact: the data feed summed four half-year filings, which is two years, so both the trailing earnings and the trailing cash flow were double-counted. The honest figures are 11.20 euros of trailing earnings per share and 2.85 billion euros of trailing free cash flow. Worse, that 2.85 billion uses a narrow capital-expenditure definition; management's own guidance is roughly 1.4 billion euros a year of capital spending across works and concessions, which takes true free cash flow to about 2.0 billion. So the real multiples are 9.8 times earnings and roughly five times honest free cash flow, a discount of about a fifth to Vinci, not a half. There is a gap. It is an ordinary gap.

Second, and decisively, roughly 70% of group profit comes from an asset with an end date. The APRR and AREA motorway concessions expire in the first half of the 2030s, and what follows is unknown. Management's own framing from the February 2025 call is the problem in their words: the regulator is pushing for shorter periods, more regulation, review clauses and additional required investment, and no clarity is expected before 2027 or 2028. A concession renewed on shorter, more regulated, more capital-hungry terms is worth a fraction of the one expiring. Valuing that stream on a low price-to-earnings multiple, as every screen does, capitalises a wasting annuity into perpetuity. Correctly valued as a finite annuity, most of the apparent cheapness disappears.

Third, the counterparty is a fiscally strained sovereign with a demonstrated willingness to reach into this exact pocket. France already levies a long-distance transport infrastructure tax on motorway operators and imposed an exceptional corporate surtax that the finance director quantified at about 200 million euros of group effect for 2025. Asked in August 2025 to size the sensitivity if corporate tax normalised, he declined to give a number, saying only that it is one of the things a government may decide in a finance law. The dividend policy, formally set at a 45% payout in February 2025 with unusual emphasis, was already being hedged six months later against exactly this. An infrastructure owner that cannot forecast its own tax rate is not a bond proxy.

Fourth, the deterioration is visible in the returns. Return on invested capital has fallen for three consecutive years, 6.80% to 6.40% to 6.17%, and invested capital actually shrank in the final year, so this is a numerator problem, not acquisition goodwill. Gross margin is contracting at 12.9%. Return on equity has slipped from 15.7% to 13.6%. Revenue growth collapsed from 7.9% to 1.0% in twelve months. French roads are shrinking 5%. And net debt of 10.88 billion euros including leases against 4.26 billion of EBITDA, with a solvency score of 1.8, is real leverage into a 30-year rate at a 19-year high.

The fifth risk is the one the company cannot touch. The first-half 2026 shortfall was caused by high oil depressing light-vehicle traffic, itself caused by an unresolved Middle East conflict. The recovery thesis therefore rests on a single macro variable no one at Eiffage controls, and with Brent near 91 dollars and diplomacy stalled, that variable is currently moving the wrong way. Confirmation of the bear case would be Brent sustained above 100 dollars with a second consecutive half of falling motorway traffic, a French finance law making the corporate surtax or the infrastructure levy permanent, or the first concrete signal that the post-2030 concession framework will be materially less generous. Any one of those takes the shares to the low 90s.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market runs in both directions here, which is unusual and is the main reason this is a wait rather than a buy.

We disagree with the bulls first. The dominant quantitative view of Eiffage, and the view embedded in the screening data handed to this committee, is that it trades at 3.6 times free cash flow with every valuation method deeply positive, a discounted-cash-flow fair value of 372 euros and margins of safety of 41% to 71%. That view is arithmetically broken. Eiffage reports half-yearly, the data feed summed four half-year filings, and both trailing earnings and trailing cash flow were consequently double-counted. Corrected, the stock is on 9.8 times earnings and about five times honest free cash flow after management's own guided 1.4 billion euros a year of capital spending. A 372 euro fair value sitting alongside a 104.75 euro Buffett-style fair value on the same page is not a disagreement between models, it is a broken model, and anyone underwriting a triple here is underwriting a spreadsheet error.

We also disagree with the way both bulls and bears value the motorway. Almost every treatment of Eiffage capitalises APRR's earnings on a multiple, as though they continue forever. They do not. APRR and AREA expire in the first half of the 2030s, and the chief executive's own account of what comes next, from 27 February 2025, is that the regulator wants shorter periods, more regulation, review clauses and more required investment, with no clarity before 2027 or 2028. Around 70% of group profit therefore comes from a wasting asset that must be valued as a finite annuity. Doing so is what takes our fair value to 135 euros rather than the 200-plus that a naive multiple on group earnings would produce.

Where we disagree with the bears, and where the genuine edge sits, is the other side of the same coin. The market is applying a French-motorway discount to the whole company. But 21.7 billion euros of the 26.3 billion euro revenue base is contracting, with an order book that has grown every single reporting period across every business line, winning nuclear, grid, offshore-wind, district-heating and data-centre work, and with Europe outside France still growing over 8% while France stalls. And roughly 2.05 billion euros of the 10.7 billion euro market value is a stake in Getlink marked at today's price, an asset with nothing to do with French motorways at all. Those parts are not getting a fair hearing. That is the mispricing, and it is worth roughly 20% rather than roughly 100%.

The last piece of consensus we would flag is a silence rather than a claim. The APRR succession question was asked once, by a BNP Paribas analyst in February 2025, and has not been raised on either subsequent call. The single largest determinant of what this company is worth has dropped out of the conversation entirely. That is either an opportunity, because no one is arguing about it, or a warning, because no one is watching it.
forcing_function:
There is no single event that forces a re-rating here, and that is the honest answer rather than a reason to score the name down.

The dated events that exist are routine. Full-year 2026 results arrive in late February 2027, roughly six months out, carrying with them the board's dividend decision under the 45% payout policy and the first full read on whether second-half motorway traffic recovered. That is a real information event with a real date, and it is the one to mark.

The development that would actually matter has no date at all. It is the publication of a concrete French framework for what follows the APRR and AREA concessions. Management's own guidance, from 27 February 2025, is that this cannot be understood before 2027 or 2028, and eighteen months later nothing has advanced. When it comes, it revalues 70% of the company's profit in one direction or the other, and there is no way to position for its timing.

The third possible forcing function is not corporate at all: a durable fall in the oil price. If Brent settles back below 80 dollars, light-vehicle motorway traffic recovers, the concessions shortfall reverses, and the second-half figures do the re-rating without any announcement. That is the most likely path to 135 euros within our eighteen-month horizon, and it is also precisely the problem, because it is a macro variable Eiffage does not control and one the current regime is actively hostile to.

A fourth is optional and undated: management has twice bought blocks of Getlink opportunistically and said in February 2025 it remains keenly interested at the right price while ruling out taking control. A further increase would be a signal about how management values its own concession assets, but it will happen when a seller appears, not on a calendar.

We would explicitly discount two things that look like forcing functions and are not. The buyback cannot force anything because the shares are warehoused, not cancelled. And activism is implausible here: Eiffage's employee shareholders hold a large, stable block, the group is a French infrastructure champion, and there is no governance failure to attack. This is not a Third Point setup.
valley_of_death:
The risky window over the next three to nine months is unusually well defined, and every element of it is external.

The first and largest is oil. The first-half 2026 shortfall was caused by high fuel prices depressing light-vehicle motorway traffic, and the chief executive named that cause directly on 26 August 2026. Brent stood near 91 dollars in mid-August after round-tripping from 100.69 dollars in late July down to 79.36 dollars on 4 August, the United States and Iran ceasefire memorandum expired on 17 August with no deal and no visible diplomacy, a cargo vessel was struck in the Strait of Hormuz, and transits are running well below pre-conflict levels under a naval blockade. Second-half motorway traffic is therefore likely to be soft again, and the second-half figures are what matter most: Eiffage's cash generation is heavily back-loaded, with 2.67 billion euros of the 2.85 billion trailing free cash flow earned in the second half of 2025 and only 187 million in the first half of 2026. A weak second half hits the one number that currently supports the whole valuation case.

The second is French fiscal policy. The exceptional corporate surtax cost the group about 200 million euros in 2025 by the finance director's own quantification, and the long-distance transport infrastructure levy already sits on motorway revenue. The autumn finance-law season is the window in which either could be extended or increased, and management has said plainly it has no more visibility than investors do. The dividend decision, taken by the board alongside full-year results in late February 2027, has already been pre-hedged twice against exactly this.

The third is rates. The 30-year United States Treasury yield hit 5.31%, a 19-year high, with no cuts priced through December and the long end selling off in an orderly, directional way rather than a panicked one. A company carrying 10.88 billion euros of net debt against 4.26 billion of EBITDA, whose principal asset is a long-duration cash-flow stream, gets valued down by exactly that move, and refinancing at the concession level becomes incrementally more expensive.

The fourth is the French domestic order book. Eiffage Route contracted 5% in the first half of 2026 on weaker local-authority ordering, with no recovery timetable offered. French municipal budgets are not about to loosen.

There is no debt-maturity wall we can identify from the disclosures and no cash-burn hump; this is a profitable, cash-generative business. The valley here is a valuation valley, not a solvency one. But note the shape of the setup: the shares are already 15% below their 200-day average and within 6% of the 52-week low, so the market has partly discounted this. What it has not discounted is a second consecutive weak half.
positioning_washout:
There is no mechanical, forced-selling dynamic here, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. Eiffage is not a former high-growth name whose shareholder register is about to be repriced, and there is no pivot, no dividend cut announced, and no index event we can identify.

What the register does have is a yield-and-value ownership profile that is vulnerable in one specific way. Eiffage yields 4.40% on a trailing dividend of 4.80 euros and a payout policy formally set at 45% of earnings in February 2025. That policy was hedged by the finance director in August 2025 against the French special tax, and the board decision lands with the full-year results in late February 2027. If that payout were cut or suspended, the income holders who own this stock for the yield would sell, and they would sell into a market that is already 15% below the 200-day average. That is the one genuine washout risk, and it is dated to late February 2027, outside our nine-month window but only just.

The positioning data we have is thin and points the same direction: a smart-money score of 10 out of 100, institutional flow neutral at 50 out of 100, and an insider buy ratio of zero. Nobody with an information advantage is buying this at 109 euros. That is not a sell signal, but it removes any argument that insiders are signalling the bottom.

One structural point cuts against any hope of a technical squeeze. Eiffage holds treasury stock of roughly 6% of its capital and has told the market explicitly, on 27 February 2025, that it will neither cancel those shares nor reduce the holding before 2027. The buyback warehouses stock rather than retiring it, so it provides a bid but no per-share arithmetic benefit and no shrinking float. Do not underwrite a squeeze that the company has pre-announced it will not create.
moderator_conclusion:
Wait for the wash-out. Eiffage is a genuinely good business at a modestly good price, and the gap between those two adjectives is the whole call.

Start with what we actually own at 109.20 euros. A legal monopoly over a French motorway network throwing off around 2.3 billion euros a year of gross operating profit at margins above 70%. A 21.7 billion euro contracting business whose order book has grown every reporting period since 2023 across every single business line, winning nuclear, grid, offshore-wind, district-heating and data-centre work across France, Germany, Spain, Poland, Belgium and the Netherlands. A fifth of Getlink, worth about 2.05 billion euros at today's price, or roughly a fifth of Eiffage's entire market value, carried in the books at far less. And a management team that has delivered three consecutive guidance commitments, flagged every disappointment in the call it occurred rather than after, and spent several minutes on its own results call arguing down the data-centre opportunity that has other builders trading at 36 times earnings. The credibility here is high and it is earned.

Now the discipline. The screening data handed to this committee said 3.6 times free cash flow with margins of safety of 41% to 71%. That was wrong: Eiffage reports half-yearly and the feed double-counted, showing 21.39 euros of trailing earnings against a true 11.20 and 5.90 billion euros of free cash flow against a true 2.85 billion, which itself falls to about 2.0 billion once management's own guided capital spending is charged. The stock is on 9.8 times earnings against Vinci's 12.5 times, a discount of about a fifth, not a half. And that fifth is partly deserved: Eiffage is more levered, more concentrated in France, and earns 6.17% on invested capital, down from 6.80% two years ago, with invested capital shrinking in the final year so the numerator is genuinely deteriorating.

More importantly, roughly 70% of group profit comes from a concession with a defined end date in the first half of the 2030s, being renegotiated with a fiscally strained state that its own chief executive says wants shorter durations, tighter regulation and more required investment, with no clarity before 2027 or 2028. That is why we value it as a finite annuity rather than a perpetuity, why our rebuilt fair value is 135 euros rather than the 200-plus a naive multiple would give, and why the moat is eroding rather than wide: a high but falling return on a licence with an expiry date is not a durable franchise, whatever the multiple says. It is worth being precise about what this is not, though. This is not a company facing secular displacement. Electrification, grid build-out, nuclear and data centres are all tailwinds to its contracting arm, and electric vehicles remove a fuel-cost drag on toll traffic without touching the toll. The terminal risk here is contractual and fiscal, not technological.

What the market regime does to this call is the deciding factor. The first-half 2026 shortfall was caused by high oil depressing motorway traffic, and management said so in plain terms on 26 August. Brent sits near 91 dollars, the United States and Iran memorandum expired on 17 August with no deal and no visible diplomacy, and the strait is operating under a naval blockade. So the path to our 135 euro fair value runs through a single shared macro variable that Eiffage does not control and that is currently moving against it. That is exactly the resolution-driver dependence this book is meant to be wary of. Meanwhile the 30-year yield is at a 19-year high with no cuts priced through December, which is the wrong tape for a levered owner of long-duration cash flows, and any thesis that quietly depends on rate relief must be marked down rather than credited. On the other side, the regime's clearest instruction is that free cash flow, not revenue growth, is now the discriminator, and on that measure Eiffage is on the right side of the line: roughly 2.0 billion euros of honest free cash flow against a 10.7 billion euro market value, a 4.40% dividend covered at a 41% payout, and margins that improved even as revenue growth fell to 1.0%.

On continuity: we last looked at this name on 24 August at 118 euros and called it a wait with moderate conviction and a 135 euro fair value. The half-year results published on 26 August are a genuine dated development, and they cut both ways. Revenue growth collapsed to 1.0% from 7.9%, French roads shrank 5%, and the chief executive answered a direct question about improved confidence with the single word no. Against that, profits rose 11%, margins improved, the order book grew again, and the shares are 7.5% cheaper. The operating case is modestly worse; the price is modestly better; they very nearly cancel. We have rebuilt the parts from scratch rather than inheriting the number, and the rebuild lands independently at 135 euros. So we keep the same call and the same conviction, which is what the continuity discipline requires when nothing dated has moved the case decisively.

At 109.20 euros the shares sit about 19% below our base case and about 16% above our adverse case. That is a real but ordinary asymmetry on an eroding-moat asset whose recovery driver is an oil price. It does not clear the bar for capital today. What would: a print below 100 euros, which breaks the 103.05 euro 52-week low and takes the discount to our base case past 26%, or a dated development on either of the two things that actually resolve this — Brent sustained below 80 dollars restoring light-vehicle traffic for a full reporting period, or the French state publishing a concrete post-2030 concession framework. Buy the wash-out or buy the clarity. Do not buy the screen.

Vinci owns ASF, Cofiroute and Escota and faces the same French state, the same long-distance transport infrastructure levy and the same corporate surtax debate.
