peer_comps_note:
The peer file's conclusion that Eiffage trades at roughly half Vinci's multiple does not survive contact with corrected data, and this is the most important correction in the note. That conclusion rests on a stated 3.6 times free cash flow, which comes from the same double-counting artefact described above: because Eiffage reports half-yearly, the feed summed four half-year filings and produced two years of earnings and cash flow. Rebuilt on live quotes taken today, 31 August 2026, the picture is far more ordinary. Eiffage at 109.20 euros trades on 9.8 times trailing earnings, about 5.1 times enterprise value to EBITDA, and yields 4.40%. Vinci, the closest and most appropriate anchor, trades at 114.20 euros on 12.5 times trailing earnings, 6.5 times enterprise value to EBITDA, 7.7 times free cash flow, and yields 4.38%. Bouygues at 44.26 euros is on 13.5 times and yields 4.74%. So the discount to Vinci is about 22% on earnings and about 22% on enterprise value to EBITDA, not about 50%. The other two names in the peer set are not usable anchors and would badly inflate the apparent gap if cited: Hochtief at 423.60 euros is on 35.9 times earnings and 14.5 times enterprise value to EBITDA, having re-rated on data-centre and Turner exposure, and Ferrovial at 50.36 euros is on 58.6 times and 26.4 times on the strength of the 407ETR toll road and its United States listing. Both are current live multiples, not remembered ones.

On how much of the remaining 22% gap is genuine single-name edge: less than it appears, and for a reason worth stating explicitly. French motorway concession risk, the political and fiscal question that most obviously explains a discount here, is a shared factor, not an Eiffage-specific one. Vinci owns ASF, Cofiroute and Escota and faces the same French state, the same long-distance transport infrastructure levy and the same corporate surtax debate. A risk both names carry cannot explain why one is cheaper than the other. What can explain it is the mix: Eiffage is more concentrated in France, is more levered (net debt of 10.88 billion euros against 4.26 billion of EBITDA), earns lower returns on invested capital at 6.17% and falling, and its concession has a nearer end date, against Vinci's diversified airports and international construction. A discount of roughly a fifth for that combination is defensible rather than absurd. Our base-case fair value of 135 euros deliberately implies 12.1 times earnings, just below Vinci's 12.5 times, because Eiffage should trade at a modest discount to Vinci on the merits, not at a premium.
interrogator_dossier:
# Eiffage S.A. (FGR.PA) — Forensic Dossier

**Prepared:** 2026-08-31 · **Listing:** Euronext Paris, quoted in euros · **Price used: €109.20** (live quote, 2026-08-31; previous close €109.70, day range €109.15–€110.40)
**Transcripts reviewed:** 2025-02-27 (2024 full-year results), 2025-08-29 (H1 2025 results), 2026-08-26 (H1 2026 results)
**Continuity:** this committee last covered Eiffage on 2026-08-24 at €118.

---

## A note on the data before anything else

Three numbers handed to this committee are wrong, and one of them is load-bearing. Eiffage reports on a half-yearly basis, not quarterly, and the data feed has summed four consecutive half-year filings — which is two full years, not one. That produces a trailing-twelve-month (TTM, the last four quarters of results) earnings-per-share figure of €21.39 and a TTM free cash flow of €5.90 billion. Both are exactly double the truth.

Rebuilt from the underlying filings:

| Item | As handed to us | Actual |
|---|---|---|
| TTM earnings per share | €21.39 | **€11.20** (H2 2025 €7.71 + H1 2026 €3.49) |
| TTM free cash flow | €5.90bn | **€2.85bn** (H2 2025 €2.67bn + H1 2026 €0.19bn) |
| Latest-period earnings per share, year on year | −13% | **+5.8%** (€3.49 vs €3.30 in H1 2025) |

At €109.20 that puts the shares on roughly **9.8 times trailing earnings**, not the low-single-digit multiple the raw feed implies. This matters enormously for the peer work in section 2, because the discount to Vinci is about a fifth, not about a half. A committee that anchored on 3.6 times cash flow would be underwriting a stock that does not exist.

A fourth figure should also be set aside: the discounted-cash-flow "fair value" of €372 carried on the stock page. Against a €104.75 Buffett-style fair value on the same page, and a share price of €109.20, that spread is not a disagreement — it is a broken model. The per-method margins of safety (+41% to +71%) inherit the same problem.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across three calls spanning eighteen months, Eiffage's management has told one story with remarkable consistency, and the story has quietly gone from being about **acceleration** to being about **holding the line**.

**February 2025 (2024 results) — the expansion chapter.** Chief executive Benoit de Ruffray opens on records: "2024, once again, a very strong year both in terms of earnings as well as order intake, these good results. What's more were accompanied by extremely good cash flow generation." The order book finishes 11% above a record 2023. The centrepiece is a change of scale in Germany — the Salvia and EQOS acquisitions taking Eiffage Energy Systems in Germany past 4,500 employees — plus €1.1bn of offshore-wind order intake at Smulders and 158 new solar plants in Spain. Group revenue grew 7.3%, of which roughly 4 percentage points was acquired. The forward-looking language is about *entering* markets: Germany, the Netherlands, Austria.

**August 2025 (H1 2025) — the consolidation chapter.** The tone is still confident but the emphasis shifts from entering to *deepening*. Revenue growth of 8.4%; Europe outside France growing 17.4%; the Construction division "back to growth" after a negative first quarter. New qualifiers appear that were absent in February: the French corporate surtax (a €200m full-year group effect, per finance director Christian Cassayre), and the first explicit hedging on the dividend — "this special tax this year, of course, you can expect that this will have an effect on dividends."

**August 2026 (H1 2026) — the defensive chapter.** The opening is no longer about records. It is about *why the trends will still be there later*: "sovereignty of energy, development of new mobilities, necessary adaptation to the climate change." That is a decade-horizon framing, and it is the sentence a management team reaches for when the current half is not the story it wants told. And it is not: the motorway business is explicitly down, and de Ruffray names the cause without softening it — "performance is impacted by the decrease of the motorway traffic of the LVs [light vehicles] given the persistence of the oil price, which is high, direct consequence of the Middle East conflict." Eiffage Route, the French roads arm, is "contracting by 5%, impacted mainly by the decrease of public order from the local authorities." Europe outside France is still growing but management flags it plainly: "As anticipated, the growth of activity is less important than in 2025."

**What was introduced and what was quietly dropped.** Introduced: data centres, discussed at length in 2026 but with unusual restraint (below). Introduced: nuclear, from a €100–200m maintenance annuity in 2025 to a twelve-year Arabelle Solutions partnership and roughly €5bn of EPR2 work in the book. Quietly de-emphasised: offshore wind, which carried the 2024 story and is now a passing mention — consistent with the caution management voiced in August 2025 about European clients "facing some challenges on the U.S. part."

**The thread that never resolves.** In February 2025 an analyst asks the question that actually determines what Eiffage is worth: how will it replace the profit the APRR motorway concession contributes when that concession ends? De Ruffray's answer is honest and unsatisfying in equal measure: the regulator "is pushing for shorter periods for more regulation with more — with review clauses… and also the need to have additional investment," and "we can't really have a final understanding of what the future model will be before 2027, 2028. And at some point, we'll be getting so close to 2031." Eighteen months and two calls later, that question has not been asked again and management has not volunteered an update. The single largest open item in the valuation is the one the calls have gone quiet on.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Where and when | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "A year of dynamic growth, plus 7.3% revenue growth" | Feb 2025 | 2024 revenue €24.02bn, +7.3% on 2023's €22.37bn. Management itself discloses ~4pp came from acquisitions, so organic was ~3.3% | **Matches, and honestly disclosed.** Management volunteered the acquired/organic split unprompted |
| "The revenues of the group is growth again at plus 8.4%" | Aug 2025 | H1 2025 revenue €12.31bn vs €11.41bn = +7.9% on the filed figures | **Matches** (the small gap is scope/currency) |
| Results "increasing outcome as expected"; 2026 outlook for higher activity and results confirmed | Aug 2026 | H1 2026 revenue €12.44bn vs €12.31bn = **+1.0%**. Operating profit €1,019m vs €982m (+3.8%). Attributable net profit €342m vs €308m (+11%) | **Technically true, materially generous.** Profit did rise. But revenue growth collapsed from 7.9% to 1.0% in twelve months and "as expected" papers over a very large deceleration |
| Group margin profile intact — "we have no notion of impairment of the margin level" | Aug 2026 | Operating margin TTM 9.96%; gross margin 12.9% and flagged as contracting by our screen. Operating profit margin H1 2026 8.2% vs 8.0% a year earlier | **Holds at the operating line.** Margins are stable-to-fractionally-better, not deteriorating. This claim survives scrutiny |
| Concessions are the quality earnings engine | All three calls | Group EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) TTM €4.26bn on €26.26bn of revenue. Backing out contracting at a normal ~6% margin implies concessions carries roughly €2.9–3.0bn of that — around 70% of group EBITDA on ~17% of revenue | **Confirmed, and it is the whole company.** Contracting is €21.7bn of revenue earning a ~4.3% operating margin. Concessions is the profit |
| "Extremely good cash flow generation" | Feb 2025 | 2024 operating cash flow €3.71bn; 2025 €3.47bn; TTM €3.44bn. Genuinely large and genuinely stable | **Confirmed** — with one caveat below |
| Capital expenditure "about €700 million for the year… and about €700 million as well in concessions" | Aug 2025 | The data feed's narrow capital-expenditure line is €352m for a half-year. The property-plant-and-equipment investment line is €730m for the same period, and management's own guided total is ~€1.4bn a year | **Management's number is the right one.** Using the feed's narrow line flatters free cash flow by roughly €1bn a year. Honest free cash flow is ~€2.0–2.3bn, not €2.85bn |
| Returns on capital | — | Return on invested capital 6.80% (2023) → 6.40% (2024) → **6.17% (2025)**. Return on equity 15.7% → 15.5% → 13.6% | **Falling, three years running** — and invested capital actually *shrank* in 2025, so this is not an acquisition-goodwill artefact. The numerator is deteriorating |
| Balance sheet | — | Net debt at 30 June 2026 of **€10.88bn** including €1.14bn of capitalised leases (€9.74bn excluding them), against €4.26bn of TTM EBITDA — about 2.6 times. Altman-Z solvency score 1.8 | **Levered, as a concession owner should be**, but the score sits in the zone that warrants monitoring |

**The single most important reconciliation.** Free cash flow of €2.85bn on a €10.70bn market value looks like a 27% yield and is the reason this name screens as spectacularly cheap. It is not. Strip in management's own €1.4bn of annual capital expenditure and the figure is roughly €2.0bn — a still-attractive but far more ordinary ~19% — and a material slice of *that* is generated by a motorway concession with a defined end date, meaning it is partly return *of* capital, not return *on* it. The cheapness is real. It is about half as large as it looks.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Declining — modestly, and from a high base.**

- **Feb 2025 — offensive.** "Very strong year," "record order book," "major scale change," "total change of scale in Germany." The verbs are about acquiring, entering, expanding. Guidance is offered freely.
- **Aug 2025 — offensive with new defensive clauses.** Still "went very well according to our expectations," but the call introduces tax uncertainty, dividend hedging, and a first note of caution on offshore wind clients. On France's tax regime Cassayre concedes: "we do not have more visibility than you have."
- **Aug 2026 — defensive.** Opens with a decade-long structural argument rather than the half's results. Names an external cause for the concessions shortfall. Concedes contraction at Eiffage Route.

The sharpest single datapoint in the entire transcript set is one word. Morgan Stanley's Nicolas Mora asks, in August 2026, whether management is "more confident, less confident? Given the order intake… More confident than in February?"

De Ruffray's complete answer: **"No."**

He then lets his colleague give the longer, warmer version, and only afterwards adds that "the assumption of 2%, 3% organic growth is the right one." A chief executive who answers a confidence question with a bare monosyllable and hands the elaboration to someone else is not signalling deterioration — he is signalling that he will not be pushed above his number. Read alongside "there's no reason to change the margin profile of the group," this is a management team that has decided to defend a range rather than raise one.

Specificity has, notably, *improved* over the period — the dividend policy was formalised at a 45% payout, capital expenditure was quantified by division, and organic-growth guidance is given as a number. Confidence is down; disclosure discipline is up. That is a good combination in a company under pressure, and it is the main reason the credibility score below is not lower.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High.** This is the strongest part of the file.

Three guidance commitments can be traced from the call where they were made to the call where they were tested:

1. **Construction back to growth in 2025.** Promised in February 2025 ("we intended to get back to growth in the volume on construction as of '25"). By August 2025: a negative first quarter, then a second quarter strong enough to more than offset it, delivering +3.6% for the half. Management flagged the first-quarter weakness in advance rather than after. **Delivered.**
2. **Second-half 2025 construction growth to continue.** Promised August 2025. Full-year 2025 revenue landed at €26.13bn, +8.8% — the strongest growth of the five-year record. **Delivered.**
3. **Energy Systems organic growth of 2–3% in 2026.** Set in February 2026, tested in August 2026 after a soft first quarter. Management neither raised nor abandoned it: "the assumption of 2%, 3% organic growth is the right one," with an explicit base-effect explanation for the weak first quarter. **On track, and defended without inflation.**

There is no sandbagging pattern and no pattern of quiet withdrawal. When something went wrong — the first-quarter 2025 construction decline, the first-quarter 2026 Energy Systems softness, the 2026 motorway traffic drop — management named it in the same call, gave the cause, and restated the target. The screen's 60% "beat" rate (three of five periods) understates this; for a company guiding on annual revenue and margin ranges rather than quarterly earnings per share, delivery against the stated ranges is the relevant test, and it has been met.

The one commitment carrying genuine doubt is the **45% dividend payout policy**. It was introduced in February 2025 with unusual firmness — "What's important in your models is to model this 45% payout policy. That's what's important." By August 2025 it was already being qualified: the policy stands, but the special tax "will have an effect on dividends," and "things are pretty unstable right now." The policy has not been broken. It has been pre-hedged.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**What is asked and answered well.** Capital expenditure, acquisition strategy, order-book quality, margin profile, nuclear exposure. Management is specific and unevasive on all of these. Cassayre's refusal to budget acquisition spending in advance ("we adjust CapEx based on opportunities as they show up") is a genuine answer, not a dodge.

**What is deflected.** French tax. Asked directly by Jefferies' Graham Hunt in August 2025 to size the impact if corporate tax returned to a normal level, Cassayre answers with process rather than arithmetic: the surtax "is temporary," there is "a piece of constitution of the quality before tax," and rate changes are "part and parcel of things that a government may decide in a financing law." He does not give the sensitivity. He may not have it. But an infrastructure owner in a country with an acute fiscal problem, declining to quantify its tax sensitivity, is a gap analysts have now stopped asking about — which is worse than them still asking.

**What analysts should be pushing on and are not.** The APRR succession question was asked once, in February 2025, by an unnamed BNP Paribas analyst, and received the "not before 2027, 2028" answer. It has not been raised on either subsequent call in this set. The largest single determinant of Eiffage's intrinsic value has fallen out of the conversation. That is a coverage failure, and for a buyer it is the most interesting fact in this dossier — the market is not currently arguing about the thing that matters.

**Where management volunteers restraint — and deserves credit.** On data centres, in August 2026, de Ruffray is asked about a €30bn opportunity set and spends several minutes arguing it *down*: only France and Germany have the teams, "we regard that we have 2 teams able to do it in France today," European permitting is slow ("they discover the red tape in Europe"), "do not expect a tremendous jump overnight in activity," and "our ability to grow our human capabilities [is] necessarily smaller than market demand." In a market where Hochtief trades at 36 times earnings substantially on data-centre enthusiasm, an executive actively deflating his own data-centre story is either exceptionally honest or exceptionally conservative. Either reading is a green flag for a capital allocator.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Returns on invested capital have fallen three consecutive years** (6.80% → 6.40% → 6.17%) while invested capital shrank in the final year — a numerator problem, not a denominator one.

🔴 **Revenue growth collapsed from +7.9% to +1.0%** between the first halves of 2025 and 2026, and management framed it as "as expected."

🔴 **The concessions shortfall has an external, unhedgeable cause.** Motorway light-vehicle traffic is down because oil is high because of a Middle East conflict. Eiffage cannot influence any link in that chain.

🔴 **French roads are contracting 5%** on weaker local-authority ordering, and management offers no timeline for recovery.

🔴 **The dividend policy has been pre-hedged twice** (August 2025) against French tax outcomes management admits it cannot forecast.

🔴 **The buyback does not shrink the share count.** Treasury stock stood at 5.8% and rising in February 2025, and Cassayre was explicit: "We're not going to cancel our share buybacks, and we're not going to cut back our treasury stock by 2027." Shares are bought and warehoused, not retired. The per-share arithmetic gets no benefit.

🔴 **Insider buying is zero** on our screen, and the smart-money score is 10 out of 100.

🟢 **Guidance has been delivered three times running**, with bad news flagged in the same call it occurred rather than after.

🟢 **The order book has grown every period across all business lines** — through a weak French housing market, a construction downturn, and a motorway traffic decline. Multi-year visibility is the genuine article here.

🟢 **Operating margins are stable-to-improving** despite the revenue slowdown — 8.2% in H1 2026 against 8.0% a year earlier.

🟢 **Management deflates its own hot story.** The data-centre restraint described above is the behaviour of people managing risk rather than a share price.

🟢 **Diversification is working where it was built.** Europe outside France still grew over 8% in H1 2026 (4.7% organic) while France stalled — the German, Polish, Spanish, Belgian and Dutch build-out of 2024–25 is doing exactly what it was bought to do.

🟢 **The Getlink stake is a real, marked, liquid asset** carried far below its market value, and management has twice added to it opportunistically.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The verb shift.** February 2025 is full of acquisition verbs — "strengthened presence," "total change of scale," "entry into order." August 2026 is full of maintenance verbs — "confirm," "remains," "goes on," "stable activity." Nothing is being hidden; the company has simply moved from a phase of buying growth to a phase of digesting it.

**"Opportunistic" is doing a lot of work.** It appears in three distinct contexts across the set — share buybacks ("we've been opportunistic. We'll continue to be opportunistic"), the Getlink stake ("we remain keenly interested in this asset prepared to up our stake depending on market opportunities, but no more than that"), and geographic expansion ("we remain opportunistic"). Eiffage has effectively told the market it will pre-commit to nothing. For a shareholder that is a double-edged disclosure: capital will not be wasted on a schedule, but neither will it be returned on one.

**A new voice in the most important seat.** Camille Bonenfant-Jeanneney took over the motorway concessions presidency in early 2025, replacing Philippe Nourry after nineteen years. Her introduction contains a small, telling line: "I'm sure that I won't be on a par with Philippe when it comes to traffic forecasts." Her background is European institutions, RATP and ENGIE — regulatory and network-utility, not toll-road operating. That is precisely the right résumé for negotiating a concession succession with the French state, and precisely the wrong one if what you needed was another decade of operating optimisation. The appointment is a signal about what Eiffage thinks the next chapter of APRR is: a negotiation, not an operation.

**Nuclear went from annuity to franchise.** In February 2025 nuclear was "€100 million, €200 million" of recurring maintenance plus €5bn of EPR2 in the book. By August 2026 it is a twelve-year Arabelle Solutions partnership manufacturing heat-exchanger components at Lauterbourg for plants across France and Europe. That is a shift from contractor to supplier — higher margin, longer duration, and almost entirely unremarked by analysts.

**Two roads diverged on capital.** Vinci buys airports. Eiffage buys German electrical contractors and a fifth of Getlink. Over eighteen months the destination of Eiffage's capital is unambiguous: European energy services, plus a strategic stake in a cross-Channel concession it says it will not control. It is building a second concession leg and a bigger contracting leg at the same time, in a country whose fiscal position may take the first one away.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE.**

This is a competently run, honestly reported, cash-generative European infrastructure group whose management delivers what it guides, flags bad news on time, refuses to inflate its hottest story, and has quietly built a genuine second growth leg in continental Europe while its domestic market softened. Nothing in three calls suggests deterioration in the quality of the business or the candour of the people running it. The credibility here is high and it is earned.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing a position:** roughly 70% of Eiffage's profits come from a motorway concession that has a defined end date in the first half of the next decade, and neither management nor the French state can yet say what — if anything — replaces it. Management's own words from February 2025 are the whole issue: the regulator wants "shorter periods for more regulation… and also the need to have additional investment," and no clarity is expected "before 2027, 2028." Eiffage is therefore not a compounder priced cheaply; it is a very good contracting business bolted to a **high-quality wasting asset**, and the correct valuation method is to value the wasting asset as a finite annuity — not to capitalise its earnings into perpetuity on a low price-to-earnings multiple. Every screen that flags this stock as extraordinarily cheap does the latter.

**Economic moat: ERODING.** The moat type is a **regulatory licence** — APRR and AREA hold a legal monopoly over their motorway network, which is about as clean a barrier to entry as exists. But it is a *wasting* licence with a contractual expiry, being renegotiated by a counterparty (the French state) that is fiscally strained and publicly committed to shorter, more heavily regulated, more investment-intensive successor terms. Alongside that, the returns evidence is unambiguous: return on invested capital has fallen 6.80% → 6.40% → 6.17% over three years with invested capital shrinking in the final year, gross margin is contracting at 12.9%, and return on equity has slipped from 15.7% to 13.6%. High but falling returns on a licence with an end date is the definition of an eroding moat, not a wide one. The contracting business alongside it has, realistically, no moat at all beyond local scale and density in French roads — it is a competent, cyclical, low-margin business earning about 4.3% at the operating line.

**Secular threat: manageable — and it is important to say which threat this is not.** Eiffage does not face a structural technology or channel displacement. Electrification, grid build-out, offshore wind, nuclear and data centres are all *tailwinds* to the contracting arm, and the company is winning work in every one of them; on the concession side, a shift to electric vehicles removes a fuel-cost drag on traffic without touching the toll. The 2026 traffic decline is oil-cyclical and management said so plainly. The genuine terminal-value risk here is **contractual and fiscal, not secular** — a concession that expires, and a sovereign that may extract more from what remains. That is a real risk and it is the one to underwrite, but it should not be dressed up as structural decline, and it does not map to any of the standard secular-decline themes.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** Neither cleanly, which is the honest answer. It is a **discount that is mostly deserved and partly not**. Deserved: a finite concession, a strained French sovereign, falling returns on capital, and a recovery driver (oil) the company does not control. Not deserved: the market is applying that discount to the *whole* company, including a €21.7bn contracting business with a record order book, real European diversification, and nothing whatsoever to do with French motorways, plus a stake in Getlink worth around €2bn against a €10.7bn market value. The mispricing, if it exists, lives in the parts that are not the toll road.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a moat that is being eroded · moat trend eroding · structural threat manageable.

bull_thesis:
The bull case is that the market is applying a French-motorway discount to a company that is only half a French motorway, and pricing the rest for nothing. At 109.20 euros Eiffage is worth 10.7 billion euros. Inside that sit three things a buyer would want. First, the APRR and AREA motorway concessions, a legal monopoly generating roughly 2.3 billion euros a year of earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation at margins above 70%, inflation-linked through the tariff formula, with about nine years left to run. Second, a contracting business (construction, infrastructure and energy systems) turning over about 21.7 billion euros a year at a 4.3% operating margin, whose order book has grown every single reporting period since 2023 across every business line, and which is winning exactly the work the next decade is going to pay for: roughly 5 billion euros of new-nuclear EPR2 work in the book, a twelve-year Arabelle Solutions partnership manufacturing nuclear heat-exchanger components, a 2 billion euro grid contract for Amprion in Germany, a 25-year Greater Paris district-heating concession signed in the first half of 2026, and a 120 million euro electrical substation for an artificial-intelligence data-centre campus at Fouju. Third, a stake of roughly 20% in Getlink, the Channel Tunnel operator, worth about 2.05 billion euros at Getlink's 18.89 euro share price today, or a fifth of Eiffage's entire market value, carried in the accounts far below that and marked at a price near Getlink's own 52-week high.

The operating evidence supports it. Europe outside France still grew more than 8% in the first half of 2026 (4.7% organically) while France stalled, which is the German, Dutch, Spanish, Belgian and Polish build-out of 2024 and 2025 doing precisely what it was bought to do. Operating margins improved to 8.2% from 8.0% even as revenue growth fell to 1.0%, so the slowdown is a volume story, not a pricing or execution story. Management has delivered three consecutive guidance commitments, has flagged every disappointment in the call it occurred rather than after, and has been actively deflating its own hottest narrative: asked about a 30 billion euro European data-centre opportunity, the chief executive spent several minutes arguing it down, noting he has two teams in France capable of a hyperscale project and that European permitting is slower than anyone expects. That is unusual and creditable behaviour in a market where Hochtief trades at 36 times earnings substantially on data-centre enthusiasm.

The valuation lever is straightforward. Corrected for the data error, Eiffage trades at 9.8 times trailing earnings and about 5.1 times enterprise value to EBITDA, against Vinci at 12.5 times earnings and 6.5 times, and Bouygues at 13.5 times. Eiffage yields 4.40% against Vinci's 4.38%, so an investor is paid the same to wait while owning the cheaper asset. Closing even part of that gap, on unchanged earnings, is worth 20% or more. The conditions that must hold are specific: oil has to come off its current 91 dollars so light-vehicle motorway traffic recovers; the French state has to refrain from a further permanent levy on infrastructure beyond the existing long-distance transport tax and the temporary corporate surtax; and the contracting order book has to convert at the 4-5% operating margin management insists is unchanged. If all three hold, the parts are worth around 175 euros.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is that Eiffage is cheap for four reasons that are all real, and that the cheapness is smaller than it looks.

Start with the arithmetic, because it is where most bulls go wrong. The headline 3.6 times free cash flow that makes this stock screen as extraordinary is an artefact: the data feed summed four half-year filings, which is two years, so both the trailing earnings and the trailing cash flow were double-counted. The honest figures are 11.20 euros of trailing earnings per share and 2.85 billion euros of trailing free cash flow. Worse, that 2.85 billion uses a narrow capital-expenditure definition; management's own guidance is roughly 1.4 billion euros a year of capital spending across works and concessions, which takes true free cash flow to about 2.0 billion. So the real multiples are 9.8 times earnings and roughly five times honest free cash flow, a discount of about a fifth to Vinci, not a half. There is a gap. It is an ordinary gap.

Second, and decisively, roughly 70% of group profit comes from an asset with an end date. The APRR and AREA motorway concessions expire in the first half of the 2030s, and what follows is unknown. Management's own framing from the February 2025 call is the problem in their words: the regulator is pushing for shorter periods, more regulation, review clauses and additional required investment, and no clarity is expected before 2027 or 2028. A concession renewed on shorter, more regulated, more capital-hungry terms is worth a fraction of the one expiring. Valuing that stream on a low price-to-earnings multiple, as every screen does, capitalises a wasting annuity into perpetuity. Correctly valued as a finite annuity, most of the apparent cheapness disappears.

Third, the counterparty is a fiscally strained sovereign with a demonstrated willingness to reach into this exact pocket. France already levies a long-distance transport infrastructure tax on motorway operators and imposed an exceptional corporate surtax that the finance director quantified at about 200 million euros of group effect for 2025. Asked in August 2025 to size the sensitivity if corporate tax normalised, he declined to give a number, saying only that it is one of the things a government may decide in a finance law. The dividend policy, formally set at a 45% payout in February 2025 with unusual emphasis, was already being hedged six months later against exactly this. An infrastructure owner that cannot forecast its own tax rate is not a bond proxy.

Fourth, the deterioration is visible in the returns. Return on invested capital has fallen for three consecutive years, 6.80% to 6.40% to 6.17%, and invested capital actually shrank in the final year, so this is a numerator problem, not acquisition goodwill. Gross margin is contracting at 12.9%. Return on equity has slipped from 15.7% to 13.6%. Revenue growth collapsed from 7.9% to 1.0% in twelve months. French roads are shrinking 5%. And net debt of 10.88 billion euros including leases against 4.26 billion of EBITDA, with a solvency score of 1.8, is real leverage into a 30-year rate at a 19-year high.

The fifth risk is the one the company cannot touch. The first-half 2026 shortfall was caused by high oil depressing light-vehicle traffic, itself caused by an unresolved Middle East conflict. The recovery thesis therefore rests on a single macro variable no one at Eiffage controls, and with Brent near 91 dollars and diplomacy stalled, that variable is currently moving the wrong way. Confirmation of the bear case would be Brent sustained above 100 dollars with a second consecutive half of falling motorway traffic, a French finance law making the corporate surtax or the infrastructure levy permanent, or the first concrete signal that the post-2030 concession framework will be materially less generous. Any one of those takes the shares to the low 90s.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market runs in both directions here, which is unusual and is the main reason this is a wait rather than a buy.

We disagree with the bulls first. The dominant quantitative view of Eiffage, and the view embedded in the screening data handed to this committee, is that it trades at 3.6 times free cash flow with every valuation method deeply positive, a discounted-cash-flow fair value of 372 euros and margins of safety of 41% to 71%. That view is arithmetically broken. Eiffage reports half-yearly, the data feed summed four half-year filings, and both trailing earnings and trailing cash flow were consequently double-counted. Corrected, the stock is on 9.8 times earnings and about five times honest free cash flow after management's own guided 1.4 billion euros a year of capital spending. A 372 euro fair value sitting alongside a 104.75 euro Buffett-style fair value on the same page is not a disagreement between models, it is a broken model, and anyone underwriting a triple here is underwriting a spreadsheet error.

We also disagree with the way both bulls and bears value the motorway. Almost every treatment of Eiffage capitalises APRR's earnings on a multiple, as though they continue forever. They do not. APRR and AREA expire in the first half of the 2030s, and the chief executive's own account of what comes next, from 27 February 2025, is that the regulator wants shorter periods, more regulation, review clauses and more required investment, with no clarity before 2027 or 2028. Around 70% of group profit therefore comes from a wasting asset that must be valued as a finite annuity. Doing so is what takes our fair value to 135 euros rather than the 200-plus that a naive multiple on group earnings would produce.

Where we disagree with the bears, and where the genuine edge sits, is the other side of the same coin. The market is applying a French-motorway discount to the whole company. But 21.7 billion euros of the 26.3 billion euro revenue base is contracting, with an order book that has grown every single reporting period across every business line, winning nuclear, grid, offshore-wind, district-heating and data-centre work, and with Europe outside France still growing over 8% while France stalls. And roughly 2.05 billion euros of the 10.7 billion euro market value is a stake in Getlink marked at today's price, an asset with nothing to do with French motorways at all. Those parts are not getting a fair hearing. That is the mispricing, and it is worth roughly 20% rather than roughly 100%.

The last piece of consensus we would flag is a silence rather than a claim. The APRR succession question was asked once, by a BNP Paribas analyst in February 2025, and has not been raised on either subsequent call. The single largest determinant of what this company is worth has dropped out of the conversation entirely. That is either an opportunity, because no one is arguing about it, or a warning, because no one is watching it.
forcing_function:
There is no single event that forces a re-rating here, and that is the honest answer rather than a reason to score the name down.

The dated events that exist are routine. Full-year 2026 results arrive in late February 2027, roughly six months out, carrying with them the board's dividend decision under the 45% payout policy and the first full read on whether second-half motorway traffic recovered. That is a real information event with a real date, and it is the one to mark.

The development that would actually matter has no date at all. It is the publication of a concrete French framework for what follows the APRR and AREA concessions. Management's own guidance, from 27 February 2025, is that this cannot be understood before 2027 or 2028, and eighteen months later nothing has advanced. When it comes, it revalues 70% of the company's profit in one direction or the other, and there is no way to position for its timing.

The third possible forcing function is not corporate at all: a durable fall in the oil price. If Brent settles back below 80 dollars, light-vehicle motorway traffic recovers, the concessions shortfall reverses, and the second-half figures do the re-rating without any announcement. That is the most likely path to 135 euros within our eighteen-month horizon, and it is also precisely the problem, because it is a macro variable Eiffage does not control and one the current regime is actively hostile to.

A fourth is optional and undated: management has twice bought blocks of Getlink opportunistically and said in February 2025 it remains keenly interested at the right price while ruling out taking control. A further increase would be a signal about how management values its own concession assets, but it will happen when a seller appears, not on a calendar.

We would explicitly discount two things that look like forcing functions and are not. The buyback cannot force anything because the shares are warehoused, not cancelled. And activism is implausible here: Eiffage's employee shareholders hold a large, stable block, the group is a French infrastructure champion, and there is no governance failure to attack. This is not a Third Point setup.
valley_of_death:
The risky window over the next three to nine months is unusually well defined, and every element of it is external.

The first and largest is oil. The first-half 2026 shortfall was caused by high fuel prices depressing light-vehicle motorway traffic, and the chief executive named that cause directly on 26 August 2026. Brent stood near 91 dollars in mid-August after round-tripping from 100.69 dollars in late July down to 79.36 dollars on 4 August, the United States and Iran ceasefire memorandum expired on 17 August with no deal and no visible diplomacy, a cargo vessel was struck in the Strait of Hormuz, and transits are running well below pre-conflict levels under a naval blockade. Second-half motorway traffic is therefore likely to be soft again, and the second-half figures are what matter most: Eiffage's cash generation is heavily back-loaded, with 2.67 billion euros of the 2.85 billion trailing free cash flow earned in the second half of 2025 and only 187 million in the first half of 2026. A weak second half hits the one number that currently supports the whole valuation case.

The second is French fiscal policy. The exceptional corporate surtax cost the group about 200 million euros in 2025 by the finance director's own quantification, and the long-distance transport infrastructure levy already sits on motorway revenue. The autumn finance-law season is the window in which either could be extended or increased, and management has said plainly it has no more visibility than investors do. The dividend decision, taken by the board alongside full-year results in late February 2027, has already been pre-hedged twice against exactly this.

The third is rates. The 30-year United States Treasury yield hit 5.31%, a 19-year high, with no cuts priced through December and the long end selling off in an orderly, directional way rather than a panicked one. A company carrying 10.88 billion euros of net debt against 4.26 billion of EBITDA, whose principal asset is a long-duration cash-flow stream, gets valued down by exactly that move, and refinancing at the concession level becomes incrementally more expensive.

The fourth is the French domestic order book. Eiffage Route contracted 5% in the first half of 2026 on weaker local-authority ordering, with no recovery timetable offered. French municipal budgets are not about to loosen.

There is no debt-maturity wall we can identify from the disclosures and no cash-burn hump; this is a profitable, cash-generative business. The valley here is a valuation valley, not a solvency one. But note the shape of the setup: the shares are already 15% below their 200-day average and within 6% of the 52-week low, so the market has partly discounted this. What it has not discounted is a second consecutive weak half.
positioning_washout:
There is no mechanical, forced-selling dynamic here, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. Eiffage is not a former high-growth name whose shareholder register is about to be repriced, and there is no pivot, no dividend cut announced, and no index event we can identify.

What the register does have is a yield-and-value ownership profile that is vulnerable in one specific way. Eiffage yields 4.40% on a trailing dividend of 4.80 euros and a payout policy formally set at 45% of earnings in February 2025. That policy was hedged by the finance director in August 2025 against the French special tax, and the board decision lands with the full-year results in late February 2027. If that payout were cut or suspended, the income holders who own this stock for the yield would sell, and they would sell into a market that is already 15% below the 200-day average. That is the one genuine washout risk, and it is dated to late February 2027, outside our nine-month window but only just.

The positioning data we have is thin and points the same direction: a smart-money score of 10 out of 100, institutional flow neutral at 50 out of 100, and an insider buy ratio of zero. Nobody with an information advantage is buying this at 109 euros. That is not a sell signal, but it removes any argument that insiders are signalling the bottom.

One structural point cuts against any hope of a technical squeeze. Eiffage holds treasury stock of roughly 6% of its capital and has told the market explicitly, on 27 February 2025, that it will neither cancel those shares nor reduce the holding before 2027. The buyback warehouses stock rather than retiring it, so it provides a bid but no per-share arithmetic benefit and no shrinking float. Do not underwrite a squeeze that the company has pre-announced it will not create.
moderator_conclusion:
Wait for the wash-out. Eiffage is a genuinely good business at a modestly good price, and the gap between those two adjectives is the whole call.

Start with what we actually own at 109.20 euros. A legal monopoly over a French motorway network throwing off around 2.3 billion euros a year of gross operating profit at margins above 70%. A 21.7 billion euro contracting business whose order book has grown every reporting period since 2023 across every single business line, winning nuclear, grid, offshore-wind, district-heating and data-centre work across France, Germany, Spain, Poland, Belgium and the Netherlands. A fifth of Getlink, worth about 2.05 billion euros at today's price, or roughly a fifth of Eiffage's entire market value, carried in the books at far less. And a management team that has delivered three consecutive guidance commitments, flagged every disappointment in the call it occurred rather than after, and spent several minutes on its own results call arguing down the data-centre opportunity that has other builders trading at 36 times earnings. The credibility here is high and it is earned.

Now the discipline. The screening data handed to this committee said 3.6 times free cash flow with margins of safety of 41% to 71%. That was wrong: Eiffage reports half-yearly and the feed double-counted, showing 21.39 euros of trailing earnings against a true 11.20 and 5.90 billion euros of free cash flow against a true 2.85 billion, which itself falls to about 2.0 billion once management's own guided capital spending is charged. The stock is on 9.8 times earnings against Vinci's 12.5 times, a discount of about a fifth, not a half. And that fifth is partly deserved: Eiffage is more levered, more concentrated in France, and earns 6.17% on invested capital, down from 6.80% two years ago, with invested capital shrinking in the final year so the numerator is genuinely deteriorating.

More importantly, roughly 70% of group profit comes from a concession with a defined end date in the first half of the 2030s, being renegotiated with a fiscally strained state that its own chief executive says wants shorter durations, tighter regulation and more required investment, with no clarity before 2027 or 2028. That is why we value it as a finite annuity rather than a perpetuity, why our rebuilt fair value is 135 euros rather than the 200-plus a naive multiple would give, and why the moat is eroding rather than wide: a high but falling return on a licence with an expiry date is not a durable franchise, whatever the multiple says. It is worth being precise about what this is not, though. This is not a company facing secular displacement. Electrification, grid build-out, nuclear and data centres are all tailwinds to its contracting arm, and electric vehicles remove a fuel-cost drag on toll traffic without touching the toll. The terminal risk here is contractual and fiscal, not technological.

What the market regime does to this call is the deciding factor. The first-half 2026 shortfall was caused by high oil depressing motorway traffic, and management said so in plain terms on 26 August. Brent sits near 91 dollars, the United States and Iran memorandum expired on 17 August with no deal and no visible diplomacy, and the strait is operating under a naval blockade. So the path to our 135 euro fair value runs through a single shared macro variable that Eiffage does not control and that is currently moving against it. That is exactly the resolution-driver dependence this book is meant to be wary of. Meanwhile the 30-year yield is at a 19-year high with no cuts priced through December, which is the wrong tape for a levered owner of long-duration cash flows, and any thesis that quietly depends on rate relief must be marked down rather than credited. On the other side, the regime's clearest instruction is that free cash flow, not revenue growth, is now the discriminator, and on that measure Eiffage is on the right side of the line: roughly 2.0 billion euros of honest free cash flow against a 10.7 billion euro market value, a 4.40% dividend covered at a 41% payout, and margins that improved even as revenue growth fell to 1.0%.

On continuity: we last looked at this name on 24 August at 118 euros and called it a wait with moderate conviction and a 135 euro fair value. The half-year results published on 26 August are a genuine dated development, and they cut both ways. Revenue growth collapsed to 1.0% from 7.9%, French roads shrank 5%, and the chief executive answered a direct question about improved confidence with the single word no. Against that, profits rose 11%, margins improved, the order book grew again, and the shares are 7.5% cheaper. The operating case is modestly worse; the price is modestly better; they very nearly cancel. We have rebuilt the parts from scratch rather than inheriting the number, and the rebuild lands independently at 135 euros. So we keep the same call and the same conviction, which is what the continuity discipline requires when nothing dated has moved the case decisively.

At 109.20 euros the shares sit about 19% below our base case and about 16% above our adverse case. That is a real but ordinary asymmetry on an eroding-moat asset whose recovery driver is an oil price. It does not clear the bar for capital today. What would: a print below 100 euros, which breaks the 103.05 euro 52-week low and takes the discount to our base case past 26%, or a dated development on either of the two things that actually resolve this — Brent sustained below 80 dollars restoring light-vehicle traffic for a full reporting period, or the French state publishing a concrete post-2030 concession framework. Buy the wash-out or buy the clarity. Do not buy the screen.
sop_breakdown:
Base case, all figures in euros, on 98.0 million shares: about 135 euros a share, against 109.20 today.

- APRR and AREA motorway concessions: 6.4 billion. Valued as what they are, a finite annuity rather than a perpetuity: roughly 1.05 billion a year of equity free cash flow (about 2.3 billion of EBITDA less around 0.3 billion of renewal capital spending, less concession-level interest, taxed at the French rate) over about nine remaining years, discounted at 9%. Only 0.1 billion is credited for renewal or handover compensation, because management's own account of the regulator's position is that any successor contract comes with shorter duration, tighter regulation and more required investment, and because a fiscally strained French state has every incentive to extract value rather than gift it.
- Other concessions: 1.2 billion (Nove, the 25-year Greater Paris heating concession signed in the first half of 2026, A'lienor, Millau, Lille airport, Portugal and Senegal).
- Getlink stake of roughly 20%, marked at market: 2.05 billion, or about 21 euros a share on its own, against Getlink's 18.89 euro share price and 10.25 billion market value today.
- Contracting: 6.5 billion. About 21.7 billion of revenue at a 4.3% operating margin gives 0.93 billion of operating profit, valued at 7.0 times, which sits between a pure contractor such as Balfour Beatty and the concession-supported multiple Vinci's construction arm implies.
- Subtotal: 16.15 billion.
- Less corporate and holding-level net debt of 1.6 billion. Note the group carries 10.88 billion of net debt including 1.14 billion of capitalised leases (9.74 billion excluding leases) at 30 June 2026; this sum-of-the-parts uses the including-leases definition, and the great majority of that debt sits inside the concession vehicles where its interest cost has already been charged against the concession cash flows above. Only the corporate and contracting remainder is deducted here, to avoid counting the same interest twice.
- Less minority interests at book: 1.3 billion.
- Equity value 13.25 billion, or about 135 euros a share.

Cross-check: 135 euros is 12.1 times trailing earnings of 11.20 euros, a small discount to Vinci's 12.5 times. That is the right relationship. Eiffage is more levered, more concentrated in France, and owns a concession with a nearer end date than Vinci's diversified airports and international construction, so its fair multiple should sit just below Vinci's, not above it. Any sum-of-the-parts that implies a premium to Vinci is wrong, which is why the earlier, more generous version of this build was cut back.
risk_reward: Downside to the adverse parts value of 92 euros; upside to the base-case parts value of 135 euros and to the favourable case of 175 euros, from 109.20 today. There is no structural floor beneath the shares: no deal terms, no tender, no net cash (Eiffage carries 10.88 billion euros of net debt), and a 4.40% dividend yield that the finance director has twice pre-hedged against French tax outcomes is not a floor. The nearest reference levels are the 52-week low of 103.05 euros and the adverse parts value below it. The asymmetry is real but not dramatic, and it is not independent: both the downside driver and the upside driver run through the same variable, the oil price and the Middle East conflict behind it.
catalyst_status_plain: a soft catalyst, no fixed date
peer_comps_note:
The peer file's conclusion that Eiffage trades at roughly half Vinci's multiple does not survive contact with corrected data, and this is the most important correction in the note. That conclusion rests on a stated 3.6 times free cash flow, which comes from the same double-counting artefact described above: because Eiffage reports half-yearly, the feed summed four half-year filings and produced two years of earnings and cash flow. Rebuilt on live quotes taken today, 31 August 2026, the picture is far more ordinary. Eiffage at 109.20 euros trades on 9.8 times trailing earnings, about 5.1 times enterprise value to EBITDA, and yields 4.40%. Vinci, the closest and most appropriate anchor, trades at 114.20 euros on 12.5 times trailing earnings, 6.5 times enterprise value to EBITDA, 7.7 times free cash flow, and yields 4.38%. Bouygues at 44.26 euros is on 13.5 times and yields 4.74%. So the discount to Vinci is about 22% on earnings and about 22% on enterprise value to EBITDA, not about 50%. The other two names in the peer set are not usable anchors and would badly inflate the apparent gap if cited: Hochtief at 423.60 euros is on 35.9 times earnings and 14.5 times enterprise value to EBITDA, having re-rated on data-centre and Turner exposure, and Ferrovial at 50.36 euros is on 58.6 times and 26.4 times on the strength of the 407ETR toll road and its United States listing. Both are current live multiples, not remembered ones.

On how much of the remaining 22% gap is genuine single-name edge: less than it appears, and for a reason worth stating explicitly. French motorway concession risk, the political and fiscal question that most obviously explains a discount here, is a shared factor, not an Eiffage-specific one. Vinci owns ASF, Cofiroute and Escota and faces the same French state, the same long-distance transport infrastructure levy and the same corporate surtax debate. A risk both names carry cannot explain why one is cheaper than the other. What can explain it is the mix: Eiffage is more concentrated in France, is more levered (net debt of 10.88 billion euros against 4.26 billion of EBITDA), earns lower returns on invested capital at 6.17% and falling, and its concession has a nearer end date, against Vinci's diversified airports and international construction. A discount of roughly a fifth for that combination is defensible rather than absurd. Our base-case fair value of 135 euros deliberately implies 12.1 times earnings, just below Vinci's 12.5 times, because Eiffage should trade at a modest discount to Vinci on the merits, not at a premium.

# Eiffage S.A. (FGR.PA) — Forensic Dossier

**Prepared:** 2026-08-31 · **Listing:** Euronext Paris, quoted in euros · **Price used: €109.20** (live quote, 2026-08-31; previous close €109.70, day range €109.15–€110.40)
**Transcripts reviewed:** 2025-02-27 (2024 full-year results), 2025-08-29 (H1 2025 results), 2026-08-26 (H1 2026 results)
**Continuity:** this committee last covered Eiffage on 2026-08-24 at €118.

---

## A note on the data before anything else

Three numbers handed to this committee are wrong, and one of them is load-bearing. Eiffage reports on a half-yearly basis, not quarterly, and the data feed has summed four consecutive half-year filings — which is two full years, not one. That produces a trailing-twelve-month (TTM, the last four quarters of results) earnings-per-share figure of €21.39 and a TTM free cash flow of €5.90 billion. Both are exactly double the truth.

Rebuilt from the underlying filings:

| Item | As handed to us | Actual |
|---|---|---|
| TTM earnings per share | €21.39 | **€11.20** (H2 2025 €7.71 + H1 2026 €3.49) |
| TTM free cash flow | €5.90bn | **€2.85bn** (H2 2025 €2.67bn + H1 2026 €0.19bn) |
| Latest-period earnings per share, year on year | −13% | **+5.8%** (€3.49 vs €3.30 in H1 2025) |

At €109.20 that puts the shares on roughly **9.8 times trailing earnings**, not the low-single-digit multiple the raw feed implies. This matters enormously for the peer work in section 2, because the discount to Vinci is about a fifth, not about a half. A committee that anchored on 3.6 times cash flow would be underwriting a stock that does not exist.

A fourth figure should also be set aside: the discounted-cash-flow "fair value" of €372 carried on the stock page. Against a €104.75 Buffett-style fair value on the same page, and a share price of €109.20, that spread is not a disagreement — it is a broken model. The per-method margins of safety (+41% to +71%) inherit the same problem.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across three calls spanning eighteen months, Eiffage's management has told one story with remarkable consistency, and the story has quietly gone from being about **acceleration** to being about **holding the line**.

**February 2025 (2024 results) — the expansion chapter.** Chief executive Benoit de Ruffray opens on records: "2024, once again, a very strong year both in terms of earnings as well as order intake, these good results. What's more were accompanied by extremely good cash flow generation." The order book finishes 11% above a record 2023. The centrepiece is a change of scale in Germany — the Salvia and EQOS acquisitions taking Eiffage Energy Systems in Germany past 4,500 employees — plus €1.1bn of offshore-wind order intake at Smulders and 158 new solar plants in Spain. Group revenue grew 7.3%, of which roughly 4 percentage points was acquired. The forward-looking language is about *entering* markets: Germany, the Netherlands, Austria.

**August 2025 (H1 2025) — the consolidation chapter.** The tone is still confident but the emphasis shifts from entering to *deepening*. Revenue growth of 8.4%; Europe outside France growing 17.4%; the Construction division "back to growth" after a negative first quarter. New qualifiers appear that were absent in February: the French corporate surtax (a €200m full-year group effect, per finance director Christian Cassayre), and the first explicit hedging on the dividend — "this special tax this year, of course, you can expect that this will have an effect on dividends."

**August 2026 (H1 2026) — the defensive chapter.** The opening is no longer about records. It is about *why the trends will still be there later*: "sovereignty of energy, development of new mobilities, necessary adaptation to the climate change." That is a decade-horizon framing, and it is the sentence a management team reaches for when the current half is not the story it wants told. And it is not: the motorway business is explicitly down, and de Ruffray names the cause without softening it — "performance is impacted by the decrease of the motorway traffic of the LVs [light vehicles] given the persistence of the oil price, which is high, direct consequence of the Middle East conflict." Eiffage Route, the French roads arm, is "contracting by 5%, impacted mainly by the decrease of public order from the local authorities." Europe outside France is still growing but management flags it plainly: "As anticipated, the growth of activity is less important than in 2025."

**What was introduced and what was quietly dropped.** Introduced: data centres, discussed at length in 2026 but with unusual restraint (below). Introduced: nuclear, from a €100–200m maintenance annuity in 2025 to a twelve-year Arabelle Solutions partnership and roughly €5bn of EPR2 work in the book. Quietly de-emphasised: offshore wind, which carried the 2024 story and is now a passing mention — consistent with the caution management voiced in August 2025 about European clients "facing some challenges on the U.S. part."

**The thread that never resolves.** In February 2025 an analyst asks the question that actually determines what Eiffage is worth: how will it replace the profit the APRR motorway concession contributes when that concession ends? De Ruffray's answer is honest and unsatisfying in equal measure: the regulator "is pushing for shorter periods for more regulation with more — with review clauses… and also the need to have additional investment," and "we can't really have a final understanding of what the future model will be before 2027, 2028. And at some point, we'll be getting so close to 2031." Eighteen months and two calls later, that question has not been asked again and management has not volunteered an update. The single largest open item in the valuation is the one the calls have gone quiet on.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Where and when | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "A year of dynamic growth, plus 7.3% revenue growth" | Feb 2025 | 2024 revenue €24.02bn, +7.3% on 2023's €22.37bn. Management itself discloses ~4pp came from acquisitions, so organic was ~3.3% | **Matches, and honestly disclosed.** Management volunteered the acquired/organic split unprompted |
| "The revenues of the group is growth again at plus 8.4%" | Aug 2025 | H1 2025 revenue €12.31bn vs €11.41bn = +7.9% on the filed figures | **Matches** (the small gap is scope/currency) |
| Results "increasing outcome as expected"; 2026 outlook for higher activity and results confirmed | Aug 2026 | H1 2026 revenue €12.44bn vs €12.31bn = **+1.0%**. Operating profit €1,019m vs €982m (+3.8%). Attributable net profit €342m vs €308m (+11%) | **Technically true, materially generous.** Profit did rise. But revenue growth collapsed from 7.9% to 1.0% in twelve months and "as expected" papers over a very large deceleration |
| Group margin profile intact — "we have no notion of impairment of the margin level" | Aug 2026 | Operating margin TTM 9.96%; gross margin 12.9% and flagged as contracting by our screen. Operating profit margin H1 2026 8.2% vs 8.0% a year earlier | **Holds at the operating line.** Margins are stable-to-fractionally-better, not deteriorating. This claim survives scrutiny |
| Concessions are the quality earnings engine | All three calls | Group EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) TTM €4.26bn on €26.26bn of revenue. Backing out contracting at a normal ~6% margin implies concessions carries roughly €2.9–3.0bn of that — around 70% of group EBITDA on ~17% of revenue | **Confirmed, and it is the whole company.** Contracting is €21.7bn of revenue earning a ~4.3% operating margin. Concessions is the profit |
| "Extremely good cash flow generation" | Feb 2025 | 2024 operating cash flow €3.71bn; 2025 €3.47bn; TTM €3.44bn. Genuinely large and genuinely stable | **Confirmed** — with one caveat below |
| Capital expenditure "about €700 million for the year… and about €700 million as well in concessions" | Aug 2025 | The data feed's narrow capital-expenditure line is €352m for a half-year. The property-plant-and-equipment investment line is €730m for the same period, and management's own guided total is ~€1.4bn a year | **Management's number is the right one.** Using the feed's narrow line flatters free cash flow by roughly €1bn a year. Honest free cash flow is ~€2.0–2.3bn, not €2.85bn |
| Returns on capital | — | Return on invested capital 6.80% (2023) → 6.40% (2024) → **6.17% (2025)**. Return on equity 15.7% → 15.5% → 13.6% | **Falling, three years running** — and invested capital actually *shrank* in 2025, so this is not an acquisition-goodwill artefact. The numerator is deteriorating |
| Balance sheet | — | Net debt at 30 June 2026 of **€10.88bn** including €1.14bn of capitalised leases (€9.74bn excluding them), against €4.26bn of TTM EBITDA — about 2.6 times. Altman-Z solvency score 1.8 | **Levered, as a concession owner should be**, but the score sits in the zone that warrants monitoring |

**The single most important reconciliation.** Free cash flow of €2.85bn on a €10.70bn market value looks like a 27% yield and is the reason this name screens as spectacularly cheap. It is not. Strip in management's own €1.4bn of annual capital expenditure and the figure is roughly €2.0bn — a still-attractive but far more ordinary ~19% — and a material slice of *that* is generated by a motorway concession with a defined end date, meaning it is partly return *of* capital, not return *on* it. The cheapness is real. It is about half as large as it looks.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Declining — modestly, and from a high base.**

- **Feb 2025 — offensive.** "Very strong year," "record order book," "major scale change," "total change of scale in Germany." The verbs are about acquiring, entering, expanding. Guidance is offered freely.
- **Aug 2025 — offensive with new defensive clauses.** Still "went very well according to our expectations," but the call introduces tax uncertainty, dividend hedging, and a first note of caution on offshore wind clients. On France's tax regime Cassayre concedes: "we do not have more visibility than you have."
- **Aug 2026 — defensive.** Opens with a decade-long structural argument rather than the half's results. Names an external cause for the concessions shortfall. Concedes contraction at Eiffage Route.

The sharpest single datapoint in the entire transcript set is one word. Morgan Stanley's Nicolas Mora asks, in August 2026, whether management is "more confident, less confident? Given the order intake… More confident than in February?"

De Ruffray's complete answer: **"No."**

He then lets his colleague give the longer, warmer version, and only afterwards adds that "the assumption of 2%, 3% organic growth is the right one." A chief executive who answers a confidence question with a bare monosyllable and hands the elaboration to someone else is not signalling deterioration — he is signalling that he will not be pushed above his number. Read alongside "there's no reason to change the margin profile of the group," this is a management team that has decided to defend a range rather than raise one.

Specificity has, notably, *improved* over the period — the dividend policy was formalised at a 45% payout, capital expenditure was quantified by division, and organic-growth guidance is given as a number. Confidence is down; disclosure discipline is up. That is a good combination in a company under pressure, and it is the main reason the credibility score below is not lower.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High.** This is the strongest part of the file.

Three guidance commitments can be traced from the call where they were made to the call where they were tested:

1. **Construction back to growth in 2025.** Promised in February 2025 ("we intended to get back to growth in the volume on construction as of '25"). By August 2025: a negative first quarter, then a second quarter strong enough to more than offset it, delivering +3.6% for the half. Management flagged the first-quarter weakness in advance rather than after. **Delivered.**
2. **Second-half 2025 construction growth to continue.** Promised August 2025. Full-year 2025 revenue landed at €26.13bn, +8.8% — the strongest growth of the five-year record. **Delivered.**
3. **Energy Systems organic growth of 2–3% in 2026.** Set in February 2026, tested in August 2026 after a soft first quarter. Management neither raised nor abandoned it: "the assumption of 2%, 3% organic growth is the right one," with an explicit base-effect explanation for the weak first quarter. **On track, and defended without inflation.**

There is no sandbagging pattern and no pattern of quiet withdrawal. When something went wrong — the first-quarter 2025 construction decline, the first-quarter 2026 Energy Systems softness, the 2026 motorway traffic drop — management named it in the same call, gave the cause, and restated the target. The screen's 60% "beat" rate (three of five periods) understates this; for a company guiding on annual revenue and margin ranges rather than quarterly earnings per share, delivery against the stated ranges is the relevant test, and it has been met.

The one commitment carrying genuine doubt is the **45% dividend payout policy**. It was introduced in February 2025 with unusual firmness — "What's important in your models is to model this 45% payout policy. That's what's important." By August 2025 it was already being qualified: the policy stands, but the special tax "will have an effect on dividends," and "things are pretty unstable right now." The policy has not been broken. It has been pre-hedged.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**What is asked and answered well.** Capital expenditure, acquisition strategy, order-book quality, margin profile, nuclear exposure. Management is specific and unevasive on all of these. Cassayre's refusal to budget acquisition spending in advance ("we adjust CapEx based on opportunities as they show up") is a genuine answer, not a dodge.

**What is deflected.** French tax. Asked directly by Jefferies' Graham Hunt in August 2025 to size the impact if corporate tax returned to a normal level, Cassayre answers with process rather than arithmetic: the surtax "is temporary," there is "a piece of constitution of the quality before tax," and rate changes are "part and parcel of things that a government may decide in a financing law." He does not give the sensitivity. He may not have it. But an infrastructure owner in a country with an acute fiscal problem, declining to quantify its tax sensitivity, is a gap analysts have now stopped asking about — which is worse than them still asking.

**What analysts should be pushing on and are not.** The APRR succession question was asked once, in February 2025, by an unnamed BNP Paribas analyst, and received the "not before 2027, 2028" answer. It has not been raised on either subsequent call in this set. The largest single determinant of Eiffage's intrinsic value has fallen out of the conversation. That is a coverage failure, and for a buyer it is the most interesting fact in this dossier — the market is not currently arguing about the thing that matters.

**Where management volunteers restraint — and deserves credit.** On data centres, in August 2026, de Ruffray is asked about a €30bn opportunity set and spends several minutes arguing it *down*: only France and Germany have the teams, "we regard that we have 2 teams able to do it in France today," European permitting is slow ("they discover the red tape in Europe"), "do not expect a tremendous jump overnight in activity," and "our ability to grow our human capabilities [is] necessarily smaller than market demand." In a market where Hochtief trades at 36 times earnings substantially on data-centre enthusiasm, an executive actively deflating his own data-centre story is either exceptionally honest or exceptionally conservative. Either reading is a green flag for a capital allocator.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Returns on invested capital have fallen three consecutive years** (6.80% → 6.40% → 6.17%) while invested capital shrank in the final year — a numerator problem, not a denominator one.

🔴 **Revenue growth collapsed from +7.9% to +1.0%** between the first halves of 2025 and 2026, and management framed it as "as expected."

🔴 **The concessions shortfall has an external, unhedgeable cause.** Motorway light-vehicle traffic is down because oil is high because of a Middle East conflict. Eiffage cannot influence any link in that chain.

🔴 **French roads are contracting 5%** on weaker local-authority ordering, and management offers no timeline for recovery.

🔴 **The dividend policy has been pre-hedged twice** (August 2025) against French tax outcomes management admits it cannot forecast.

🔴 **The buyback does not shrink the share count.** Treasury stock stood at 5.8% and rising in February 2025, and Cassayre was explicit: "We're not going to cancel our share buybacks, and we're not going to cut back our treasury stock by 2027." Shares are bought and warehoused, not retired. The per-share arithmetic gets no benefit.

🔴 **Insider buying is zero** on our screen, and the smart-money score is 10 out of 100.

🟢 **Guidance has been delivered three times running**, with bad news flagged in the same call it occurred rather than after.

🟢 **The order book has grown every period across all business lines** — through a weak French housing market, a construction downturn, and a motorway traffic decline. Multi-year visibility is the genuine article here.

🟢 **Operating margins are stable-to-improving** despite the revenue slowdown — 8.2% in H1 2026 against 8.0% a year earlier.

🟢 **Management deflates its own hot story.** The data-centre restraint described above is the behaviour of people managing risk rather than a share price.

🟢 **Diversification is working where it was built.** Europe outside France still grew over 8% in H1 2026 (4.7% organic) while France stalled — the German, Polish, Spanish, Belgian and Dutch build-out of 2024–25 is doing exactly what it was bought to do.

🟢 **The Getlink stake is a real, marked, liquid asset** carried far below its market value, and management has twice added to it opportunistically.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The verb shift.** February 2025 is full of acquisition verbs — "strengthened presence," "total change of scale," "entry into order." August 2026 is full of maintenance verbs — "confirm," "remains," "goes on," "stable activity." Nothing is being hidden; the company has simply moved from a phase of buying growth to a phase of digesting it.

**"Opportunistic" is doing a lot of work.** It appears in three distinct contexts across the set — share buybacks ("we've been opportunistic. We'll continue to be opportunistic"), the Getlink stake ("we remain keenly interested in this asset prepared to up our stake depending on market opportunities, but no more than that"), and geographic expansion ("we remain opportunistic"). Eiffage has effectively told the market it will pre-commit to nothing. For a shareholder that is a double-edged disclosure: capital will not be wasted on a schedule, but neither will it be returned on one.

**A new voice in the most important seat.** Camille Bonenfant-Jeanneney took over the motorway concessions presidency in early 2025, replacing Philippe Nourry after nineteen years. Her introduction contains a small, telling line: "I'm sure that I won't be on a par with Philippe when it comes to traffic forecasts." Her background is European institutions, RATP and ENGIE — regulatory and network-utility, not toll-road operating. That is precisely the right résumé for negotiating a concession succession with the French state, and precisely the wrong one if what you needed was another decade of operating optimisation. The appointment is a signal about what Eiffage thinks the next chapter of APRR is: a negotiation, not an operation.

**Nuclear went from annuity to franchise.** In February 2025 nuclear was "€100 million, €200 million" of recurring maintenance plus €5bn of EPR2 in the book. By August 2026 it is a twelve-year Arabelle Solutions partnership manufacturing heat-exchanger components at Lauterbourg for plants across France and Europe. That is a shift from contractor to supplier — higher margin, longer duration, and almost entirely unremarked by analysts.

**Two roads diverged on capital.** Vinci buys airports. Eiffage buys German electrical contractors and a fifth of Getlink. Over eighteen months the destination of Eiffage's capital is unambiguous: European energy services, plus a strategic stake in a cross-Channel concession it says it will not control. It is building a second concession leg and a bigger contracting leg at the same time, in a country whose fiscal position may take the first one away.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE.**

This is a competently run, honestly reported, cash-generative European infrastructure group whose management delivers what it guides, flags bad news on time, refuses to inflate its hottest story, and has quietly built a genuine second growth leg in continental Europe while its domestic market softened. Nothing in three calls suggests deterioration in the quality of the business or the candour of the people running it. The credibility here is high and it is earned.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing a position:** roughly 70% of Eiffage's profits come from a motorway concession that has a defined end date in the first half of the next decade, and neither management nor the French state can yet say what — if anything — replaces it. Management's own words from February 2025 are the whole issue: the regulator wants "shorter periods for more regulation… and also the need to have additional investment," and no clarity is expected "before 2027, 2028." Eiffage is therefore not a compounder priced cheaply; it is a very good contracting business bolted to a **high-quality wasting asset**, and the correct valuation method is to value the wasting asset as a finite annuity — not to capitalise its earnings into perpetuity on a low price-to-earnings multiple. Every screen that flags this stock as extraordinarily cheap does the latter.

**Economic moat: ERODING.** The moat type is a **regulatory licence** — APRR and AREA hold a legal monopoly over their motorway network, which is about as clean a barrier to entry as exists. But it is a *wasting* licence with a contractual expiry, being renegotiated by a counterparty (the French state) that is fiscally strained and publicly committed to shorter, more heavily regulated, more investment-intensive successor terms. Alongside that, the returns evidence is unambiguous: return on invested capital has fallen 6.80% → 6.40% → 6.17% over three years with invested capital shrinking in the final year, gross margin is contracting at 12.9%, and return on equity has slipped from 15.7% to 13.6%. High but falling returns on a licence with an end date is the definition of an eroding moat, not a wide one.
